density.note: The sheet prints this as a specific gravity, a density relative to water, and marks it as the figure for 70%. It prints no temperature. At two figures a specific gravity and a density in grams for each millilitre are the same number.

family.reason: The article calls 2-propanol a polar molecule that mixes with water in all proportions, and the handout has rubbing alcohol mix with water and stay apart from a vegetable oil. So on this bench, where it is also about a third water, it sorts with water. The article says too that the alcohol itself dissolves many oils: its molecule has an oily part, and the note of part 3 says so.

offBench.rationale: No source that was read says what rubbing alcohol of about 70% and mineral oil show together. What an alcohol in water does with an oil depends on how much water is in it, so no rule for a family settles it; and the supplier's sheet gives mineral oil a density of 0.845 to 0.860 g/mL, within 0.03 g/mL of the rubbing alcohol's 0.87. The pair is left off the bench (spec 25.1).

No source that was read says what a little salt does in rubbing alcohol of about 70%. The supplier's sheet says that sodium chloride dissolves slightly in alcohol, with no strength given; the article on 2-propanol says that salt can drive the alcohol out of its mixture with water as a layer of its own. What is seen would turn on the amount of salt. It is left off the bench (spec 25.1).

No source that was read says what a little sugar does in rubbing alcohol of about 70%. The supplier's sheet says that sucrose dissolves slightly in alcohol, with no strength given, and the bottle is about a third water. It is left off the bench (spec 25.1).

questions.asks: Cooking grease is oily: its molecules have no charged ends. A greasy pan is rinsed with plain water. What does the grease do?

answer.reason: The textbook page says that water does not dissolve the non-polar molecules of grease and of oil.

questions.asks: Epsom salt is a salt: like table salt, it is made of charged particles. A little is shaken into mineral oil. What does it do?

answer.reason: The article says that ionic compounds such as inorganic salts dissolve only in very polar liquids such as water. That Epsom salt is such a salt, magnesium sulfate, is not read in a source of this lab: the question states it, and the rule is asked of what the question states.

sharedNote.rationale: The note that the water, the vinegar, the two oils, the salt and the sugar share (spec 25.3). It is the red cabbage pH lab's note for foods on a bench (spec 21.4), in that lab's wording: the build copies it from that lab's record, so the two cannot come to differ. It rests on no document: makers' labels differ, and the lab cannot know whose product is on a bench.

notes.value: Two liquids that mix in any amounts are called miscible. Two that go back to layers are immiscible, and shaking does not change that.
Where a tube had two layers, the less dense liquid was the one on top.
A solid that dissolves in a liquid is called soluble in it. One that stays at the bottom is insoluble in it. The same solid can be both: it depends on the liquid.
Like dissolves like. Liquids whose molecules have charged ends, as water’s have, mix with each other and dissolve salt and sugar. Oily liquids mix with each other and with little else.
Rubbing alcohol went with water on this bench. Its molecule has a water-like end and an oily part too, and the alcohol with no water in it dissolves many oils.

neededPairs.rationale: The first part is done when six pairs of liquids count (spec 25.1); the rest are there to try. The bench offers nine.

neededSolids.rationale: The second part is done when six tubes of a solid in a liquid count (spec 25.1); the rest are there to try. The spec has six of ten; the bench offers eight, since neither solid is tried in the rubbing alcohol.

leastDensityGap.rationale: In g/mL. A pair that makes two layers is on the bench only where the two stored densities differ by at least this much. The densities are for 20 °C, for 25 °C and, for two liquids, for no stated temperature, and products differ by maker, so a smaller difference would not be taken to say which liquid floats. The least difference on the bench is 0.053 g/mL, between the rubbing alcohol and the vegetable oil.

moreMicrolitres.rationale: The liquid there is more of in a tube of two is taken as 3 mL, so that a tube can be drawn to its level and the thicker layer told from the thinner. Nothing else is worked out from it.

lessMicrolitres.rationale: The liquid there is less of in a tube of two is taken as 1.5 mL, half the other. Two liquids that mix are drawn as one liquid of the two volumes added together, which is the lab's own: a real mixture of an alcohol and water takes up a little less.

solidTubeMicrolitres.rationale: The liquid a solid is tried in is taken as 3 mL, so that the tube can be drawn to its level. Nothing is worked out from it. The solid is a little, enough to see, and no amount is stored.

unsettledUntilStood.rationale: 1 for yes. Until a tube has been shaken and has stood, the lab draws what is in it as one cloudy, unsettled liquid, with any solid spread through it, whatever the tube holds. That is the lab's own and is no claim about any pair: it keeps a tube from being read before it has stood, and makes every tube look alike until then.

mixedKeepsColour.rationale: 1 for yes. Where the pale yellow oil mixes with a liquid of no colour, the lab draws the one liquid pale yellow. That is the lab's own: no source was read for the colour of a mixture, and no answer rests on it.
